blocks.text: One Third of Florida's Banks and Credit Unions Not Yet Protected Against Future Quantum Decryption, Open-Source Scan Finds
Manteiga Foundation publishes a state-of-readiness note on 81 Florida institutions and a free scanner that tests any host in a second

runs.text: Of 81 Florida-headquartered banks and credit unions, 54 already protect their customers' connections against future quantum decryption and 27 do not yet, according to a state-of-readiness note published today by Manteiga Foundation, a Florida public benefit company. The note, the first from the foundation's Quantum Ready Labs, lists every institution with its result: quantumreadylabs.com/studies/florida-financial-2026q4.

blocks.text: Nothing is broken today. No account, login or transaction is at risk from what the note describes; every connection tested is encrypted with algorithms no existing computer can break. The question is about recordings: traffic captured now can be stored and decrypted once a large enough quantum computer exists (harvest now, decrypt later). NIST has set 2030 and 2035 as the dates for retiring today's key exchange, and browsers already negotiate a hybrid post-quantum key exchange by default.

The note sorts each institution into one of four stages, in plain words rather than letter grades: 10 do not offer TLS 1.3 at all (Exposed); 17 offer TLS 1.3 without a post-quantum key exchange (At risk); 30 accept a hybrid post-quantum key exchange (Protected); 24 add the foundations for what comes next (Ready). The median score is 85 of 100. For the 10 Exposed, the next step is to enable TLS 1.3; for the 17 At risk, to enable the X25519MLKEM768 key exchange, on current servers and content-delivery networks a configuration line or a toggle.

"Nothing is broken today, and that is exactly why this is the moment to act," said [FULL NAME], [TITLE] of Manteiga Foundation. "Confidentiality is the urgent part of the quantum transition, the fix is small, and most of these institutions are one setting away. We built the scanner so that anyone, not only specialists, can see where a host stands in under a second and what to do next."

Quantum Ready Labs is free and open source under the MIT licence. Typing a host name at quantumreadylabs.com opens a handful of TLS connections to it, as a browser visit would, and returns the stage, a score for quantum readiness alone, the one next step and the standards cited (NIST IR 8547, FIPS 203, CNSA 2.0), shareable by link or as a five-page PDF; an open API runs the same test for services and agents. On certificates the report is deliberately calm: none on the public web can be quantum-safe yet, and it says so.

Each institution's public primary domain was tested on October 18, 2026 with fourteen TLS handshakes and one ordinary connection; no page was opened and no login attempted. Every Exposed result was cross-checked with OpenSSL and curl. The population, compiled from public regulator lists with each domain verified, will be re-scanned each quarter; any institution can run a fresh test at once.
For organizations that want help making the change, the foundation operates N30.ai, its cybersecurity consulting practice. The scanner and its results remain free and open.

Manteiga Foundation is a Florida public benefit company at the meeting of technology and art, bringing more beauty into technology through open-source tools for the public good, among them Quantum Ready Labs and medet.ink. More at manteiga.org.
N30.ai is the cybersecurity consulting practice of Manteiga Foundation for the post-quantum transition and related security work. More at n30.ai.
